And researchers have found that online hoaxes spread 10 times faster than accurate stories. Now, we're also drawn to information that aligns with our viewpoints. "Psychologists call that tendency ""confirmation bias."

passages.title: MENYO passage 817
paragraphs: Ẹ lè wòye pé fọ́rán ayédèrú yẹn máa fa rògbòdìyàn tako àwọn ọmọ ogun wọ̀nyẹn. Tó bá ṣe wí pé lọ́jọ́ kejì gangan fọ́rán ayédèrú mìíràn tún jáde, tó ń ṣàfihàn ìmáámù ilú-mọ̀ọ́ká kan tó ń gbé ní London tó wá ń gbóríyìn fún ìkọlù àwọn ọmọ ogun wọ̀yẹn ńkọ́? A lè rí rògbòdìyàn àti ìfẹ̀hónúhàn, kìí ṣe ní orílẹ̀-ède Afganistan àti United kingdom nìkan, ṣùgbọ́n káàkiri gbogbo àgbáyé.

"Ẹ dẹ̀ lè sọ fúnmi wí pé, ""wá, Danielle, ìyen ò ṣe é ṣe." Ṣùgbọ́n kò rí bẹ́ẹ̀. A ti rí bí irọ́ ṣe ń tànká lórí ìkàni WhatsApp àti àwọn ìkànì àtẹ̀jíṣẹ́ mìíràn lórí ẹ̀rọ ayélukára ṣe ń yọrí sí rògbòdìyàn tako àwọn ìran kékèké.
en: You can imagine that that deepfake would provoke violence against those soldiers. And what if the very next day there's another deepfake that drops, that shows a well-known imam based in London praising the attack on those soldiers? We might see violence and civil unrest, not only in Afganistan and the United Kingdom, but across the globe.

"And you might say to me, ""Come on, Danielle, that's far-fetched." But it's not. We've seen falsehoods spread on WhatsApp and other online message services lead to violence against ethnic minorities.

passages.title: MENYO passage 818
paragraphs: Ṣe a ó kò tẹ̀síwájú ní ọ̀nà àìṣe é gbáralé àti ìgbàgbọ ohun tí a fẹ́ gbàgbọ́, ká ṣépè fún òtítọ́? Kìí ṣe wí pé a lè gba ayédèrú gbọ́ nìkan, a lè bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí sọ ìgbàgbọ́ nù nínu òtítọ́. A ti rí àwọn ènìyàn tí wọ́n lo fọ́rán ayédèrú láti sọ àríyànjiyàn sí èrí gidi nípa àṣìṣe wọn.

"A ti gbọ́ tí àwọn olóṣèlú sọ nípa fọ́rán ọ̀rọ wọn tó bani lọ́kàn jẹ́, ""Ẹ wá, ìròyìn ayédèrú nìyẹn." Ẹ ò lè gba ǹkan tí ojú àti etí yín ń sọ fún yín gbọ́. """ Ewu yẹn ni èmi àti ọ̀jọ̀gbọ́n Robert Chesney pè ní ""ère onírọ́"": ewu pé àwọn onírọ́ lè lo fọ́rán ayédèrú láti sá fún ìjíyìn àṣìṣe wọn."
en: Will we just proceed along the path of least resistance and believe what we want to believe, truth be damned? And not only might we believe the fakery, we might start disbelieving the truth. We've already seen people invoke the phenomenon of deepfakes to cast doubt on real evidence of their wrongdoing.

"We've heard politicians say of audio of their disturbing comments, ""Come on, that's fake news." You can't believe what your eyes and ears are telling you. "And it's that risk that professor Robert Chesney and I call the liar's dividend"": the risk that liars will invoke deepfakes to escape accountability for their wrongdoing."

passages.title: MENYO passage 819
paragraphs: Ní báyìí, a ti wà nínú àpérò gbogbogbò nípa ojúṣe àwọn ilé-iṣẹ́ ìmọ̀-ẹ̀rọ. Ìmọ̀ran mi fún àwọn ìkànì ìbánidọ́rẹ̀ ni láti ṣe àyípadà àdéhun iṣẹ́ wọn àti ìlànà ìtọ́sọ́nà àwùjọ láti fi òfin de fọ́rán ayédèrú tó lè fa ewu. Ìpinnu yẹn, yóò gba ìdájọ́ ọmọ ènìyàn, ó dẹ̀ wọ́n.

Ṣùgbọ́n a nílò kí àwọn ènìyán wo àkónú àti ọ̀gangan ipòo fọ́rán ayédèrú láti ṣàwárí rẹ̀ bóyá ayédèrú ènìyàn tó léwu ni tàbí dípò bẹ́ẹ̀, tí ó bá jẹ́ pé èébú tó níye lóri ni, ọgbọ́n àtinúdá tàbí ẹ̀kọ́. Ní báyìí, òfin ńkọ́? Olùdánilẹ́kọ̀ wa ni òfin jẹ́.
en: So now, we're right now engaged in a very public conversation about the responsibility of tech companies. And my advice to social media platforms has been to change their terms of service and community guidelines to ban deepfakes that cause harm. That determination, that's going to require human judgment, and it's expensive.

But we need human beings to look at the content and context of a deepfake to figure out if it is a harmful impersonation or instead, if it's valuable satire, art or education. So now, what about the law? Law is our educator.

passages.title: MENYO passage 820
paragraphs: Káàkiri àgbáyé, a ò ní òfin tó dúróo re tí wọn yóò ṣe lọ́jọ̀ láti tako ayédèrú ènìyan díjítà tó ń tú ìkọ̀kọ̀ ìbálópọ̀, tó ń ba ọmọlúwàbí ènìyàn jẹ́ tó sì ń fa ìnira inú ọpọlọ. Ǹkan tí ó ṣẹlẹ̀ sí Ranna Ayyub túbọ̀ ń ṣẹlẹ̀ si lemọ́-lemọ́. Síbẹ̀, nígbà tó lọ sí ọ̀dọ̀ àwọn agbófinró ní Delhi, wọ́n sọ fún un wí pé kò sí ǹkan tí wọ́n lè ṣe.

Òótọ́ tó bani lọ́kàn jẹ́ ni wí pé ǹkan kan náà ni yóò ṣẹlẹ̀ ní Amẹ́ríkà àti ilẹ̀ Yúróòpù. A ní àlàfo òfin tó nílò dídí. Èmi àti akẹgbẹ́ mi Dr. Mary Anne Franks ń ṣiṣẹ́ pẹ̀lú àwọn aṣòfin orílẹ̀-ède US láti ṣe òfin tí yóò fòfin de ayédèrú ènìyan díjítà tó léwu tó dọ́gba pẹ̀lú jíjí ìdánimọ̀.
en: Across the globe, we lack well-tailored laws that would be designed to tackle digital impersonations that invade sexual privacy, that damage reputations and that cause emotional distress. What happened to Rana Ayyub is increasingly commonplace. Yet, when she went to law enforcement in Delhi, she was told nothing could be done.

And the sad truth is that the same would be true in the United States and in Europe. So we have a legal vacuum that needs to be filled. My colleague Dr. Mary Anne Franks and I are working with US lawmakers to devise legislation that would ban harmful digital impersonations that are tantamount to identity theft.

passages.title: MENYO passage 821
paragraphs: Irinṣẹ́ tó kúnu ni. A dẹ̀ ní láti fi ọgbọ́n lò ó. Ó tún ní àwọn ìdíwọ́ àṣeémúlò kànkan.

Ẹ ò lè lo agbára òfin tako àwọn ènìyàn tí ẹ ò dámọ̀ tí ẹ ò lè rí. Tí oníwà-ìbàjẹ́ kan bá ń gbé ní ìta orílẹ̀-èdè níbi tí ẹni tọ́rọ̀ ṣẹlẹ̀ sí ń gbé, ẹ lè má lè takú wí pé kí oníwà-ìbàjẹ́ náà wá sí ilé-ẹjọ́ agbègbè láti kojú òfin. A máa nílò ìdáhùn láti ilẹ̀-òkèrè tó létò.
en: It's a blunt instrument. And we've got to use it wisely. It also has some practical impediments.

You can't leverage law against people you can't identify and find. And if a perpetrator lives outside the country where a victim lives, then you may not be able to insist that the perpetrator come into local courts to face justice. And so we're going to need a coordinated international response.

passages.title: MENYO passage 822
paragraphs: "Ní ọ̀pọ̀ ìgbà wọ́n máa ń sọ fún àwọn tó lúgbàdì pé, ""kọ̀ pa ẹ̀rọ kọ̀mpútà rẹ." Mójú kúrò níbẹ̀. Ó máa lọ.
A dẹ̀ rí ìyẹn nínú ìgbẹ̀jọ́ọ Rana Ayyub. "Wọ́n sọ fún-un pé, ""Wá, ó ń sọ ǹkan yìí di bàbàrà." Àwọn ọmọkùnrin ni wọ́n ń ṣìṣe ọmọkùnrin.
en: "And so often they told victims, ""Just turn your computer off." Ignore it. It'll go away.
And we saw that in Rana Ayyub's case. "She was told, ""Come on, you're making such a big deal about this." It's boys being boys.

passages.title: MENYO passage 823
paragraphs: Ó máa ń ní ìbẹ̀rù lemọ́lemọ́, pàápàá jùlọ tí ẹnìkan tí kò mọ̀ rí bá gbìyànjú láti ya àwòran rẹ̀. """Tó bá jẹ́ wí pé wọ́n fẹ́ ṣe fọ́rán ayédèrú míràn ńkọ́? "" ó máa ń ròó lọ́kan ara rẹ̀." Fún ànfàní àwọn ènìyàn bi Rana Ayyub àti fún ànfàní ìjọba àwarawa, a nílò láti ṣe ǹkan nísinyìí.
Ẹ ṣeun. Ǹkan tí àwọn ilé-iṣẹ́ ìmọ̀-ẹ̀rọ mọ̀ nípa àwọn ọmọọ̀ yín. Lójoojúmọ́, lọ́sọ̀ọ̀sẹ̀, a máa ń gba àwọn àdéhùn àti àsọtẹ́lẹ̀.
en: And she has frequent panic attacks, especially when someone she doesn't know tries to take her picture. What if they're going to make another deepfake? she thinks to herself. And so for the sake of individuals like Rana Ayyub and the sake of our democracy, we need to do something right now.
Thank you. What tech companies know about your kids Every day, every week, we agree to terms and conditions.

passages.title: MENYO passage 824
paragraphs: Mo bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí nífẹ̀ nínu ìbéérè yìí ní ọdún 2015 nígbà tí mo mọ̀ pé ọ̀pọ̀ -- ní iye ìtọpa dátà tí ènìyàn ò lérò tí wọ́n ń pèsè tí wọ́n sì ńgbà nípa àwọn ọmọ. Mo bẹ̀rẹ̀ àkànṣe iṣẹ́-ìwádìí, tí wọ́n ń pè ní Dáta Omọ onílù, mo sì pinnu láti dí àlàfo náà. Ní báyìí ẹ lè máa rò ó wí pé mo wá síbí láti dáa yín lẹ́bi fún fífi àwòrán àwọn ọmọ yín sórí ìkàni ayélukára, ṣùgbọ́n kókó ọ̀rọ̀ ibẹ̀ kọ́ nìyẹn.
"Wàhálà yìí tóbi ju ǹkan tí wọ́n ń pè ní ""fífi àwòran ọmọ sórí ìkàni ayélukára lọ." Èyí jẹ́ nípa ètò, kìí ṣe àwọn ènìyàn. Ìwọ àti ìwà rẹ ò lẹ́bi.
en: And I started to become interested in this question in 2015 when I suddenly realized that there were vast -- almost unimaginable amounts of data traces that are being produced and collected about children. So I launched a research project, which is called Child Data Citizen, and I aimed at filling in the blank. Now you may think that I'm here to blame you for posting photos of your children on social media, but that's not really the point.
"The problem is way bigger than so-called ""sharenting." This is about systems, not individuals. You and your habits are not to blame.

passages.title: MENYO passage 825
paragraphs: Wọ́n ń tọpa wọn pẹ̀lú àwọn àkọsílẹ lórí ìkọ̀nì ayélukára àti àwọn ẹ̀ka orí ẹ̀rọ ayélukára ní ọ́fíísì oníṣégùn-òyìnbo wọn. Wọ́n ń tọpa wọn pẹ̀lú àwọn ǹkan-ìṣeré wọn tí wọ́n sopọ̀ pẹ̀lu ìkàni ayélukára, àwọn ayò orí ẹ̀rọ ayélukára, àti àwọn ẹ̀rọ tó pọ̀ púpọ̀ mìíràn. "Lásíkò ìwádìí mi, ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ àwọn òbí ni wọ́n wá bámi wọ́n sì ń sọ pé, ""kí wá ni?"
Kí ló jẹ́ pàtàkì tí wọ́n bá ń tọpa àwọn ọmọ mi? A ò ní ǹkankan láti fi pamọ́. Ó dáa, Ó ṣe pàtàkì.
en: They're tracked by online records and online portals at their doctor's office. They're tracked by their internet-connected toys, their online games and many, many, many, many other technologies. "So during my research, a lot of parents came up to me and they were like, ""So what?"
Why does it matter if my children are being tracked? We've got nothing to hide. Well, it matters.

passages.title: MENYO passage 826
paragraphs: Àwọn ìmọ̀-ẹ̀rọ wọ̀nyí ni wọ́n ń lò níbi gbogbo. Ilé-ìfowópamọ́ ń lò wọ́n láti ṣe ìpinnu ẹ̀yáwó. Àwọn adójútófò ń lò wọ́n láti ṣe ìpinnu owó ìdójútófò.

Àwọn tó ń gbá òṣìṣẹ́ àti àwọn tó ń gba ènìyàn sísẹ́ máa ń lò wọ́n láti ṣe ìpinnu bóyá ènìyán tọ́ fún ìṣẹ́ kan tàbí bẹ́è kọ́. Bákan náà àwọn ọlọ́pà àti ilé-ẹjọ́ máa ń lò wọ́n láti mọ̀ bóyá ó ṣe é ṣe kí ènìyán hu ìwà ọ̀daràn tàbí ó ṣe é ṣe kí ènìyán tún ìwà ọ̀daran hù. A ò nímọ̀ kankan tàbí àkóso lórí ọ̀nà tí àwọn tó ń rà, tà tí wọ́n sì ń lo dátà wa ṣe ń ṣe àkọsílẹ̀ wa àti àwọn ọmọ wa.
en: And these technologies are used everywhere. Banks use them to decide loans. Insurance uses them to decide premiums.

Recruiters and employers use them to decide whether one is a good fit for a job or not. Also the police and courts use them to determine whether one is a potential criminal or is likely to recommit a crime. We have no knowledge or control over the ways in which those who buy, sell and process our data are profiling us and our children.

passages.title: MENYO passage 827
paragraphs: Wọ́n sì ń ta àwọn àkọsílẹ̀ wọ̀nyí pẹ̀lú orúkọ ọmọ náà, àdírẹ́si ilée wọn àti àwọn ọ̀nà ìkànsíra-ẹni fún oríṣiríṣi ilé-iṣẹ́, pẹ̀lú àwọn ilé-iṣẹ́ òwò àti iṣẹ́-ìṣe, àwọn ilé-iṣẹ́ owó-ẹ̀yá fún akẹ́kọ̀ọ́ àti ike ìgbawó àwọn akẹ́kọ̀ọ́. Láti kọjá ẹnu àlà, àwọn oníwádìí ní Fordham sọ fún oníṣòwo dátà ẹ̀kọ́ kan pé kó pèsè àkọ́jọpọ̀ àwọn ọmọbìnrin lábẹ́ ọdún mẹ́rìnlá sí mẹ́ẹ̀dógún tí wọ́n nífẹ̀ẹ́ síìfètòsẹ́bí fún wọn. Oníṣòwo dátà náà sì gbà láti pèse àkójọpọ̀ náà fún wọn.

Ẹ ronú sí irú àṣírí àti àyanjúràn tí èyí jẹ́ fún àwọn ọmọ wa. Ṣùgbọ́n àpẹẹrẹ lásán ni àwọn oníṣòwo dátà ẹ̀kọ́ jẹ́. Ọ̀títọ́ ibẹ̀ ni wí pé wọ́n ń ṣe àkọsílẹ̀ àwọn ọmọ wa ní ọ̀nà tí a ò lè darí rẹ̀ ṣùgbọ́n tí ó lẹ̀ ní ipa pàtàkì lára ànfàni wọn nílé ayé.
en: And then they sell these profiles together with the name of the kid, their home address and the contact details to different companies, including trade and career institutions, student loans and student credit card companies. To push the boundaries, the researchers at Fordham asked an educational data broker to provide them with a list of 14-to-15-year-old girls who were interested in family planning services. The data broker agreed to provide them the list.

So imagine how intimate and how intrusive that is for our kids. But educational data brokers are really just an example. The truth is that our children are being profiled in ways that we cannot control but that can significantly impact their chances in life.

passages.title: MENYO passage 828
paragraphs: Gẹ́gẹ́ bi onímọ̀ nípa àjọṣepọ̀ ènìyàn láwùjọ, mo nígbàgbọ́ wí pé ìmọ̀-àtọwọ́dá àti ìyànàná àsọtẹ́lẹ̀ lè dára lóòtó láti sọ àsọtẹ́lẹ̀ okùnfa ààrùn kan tàbí láti gbógun ti àyípadà ojú-ọjọ́. Ṣùgbọ́n a nílò láti ṣe àgbétì ìgbàgbọ́ wí pé àwọn ìmọ̀-ẹ̀rọ wọ̀nyí lè ṣe àkọsílẹ̀ àwọn ènìyàn láìṣẹ̀gbè àti wí pé a lè gbára léwọn láti fún wa ní ìpinnu nípasẹ̀ dátà nípa ìgbésíayé ènìyàn. Nítorí wọn ò lè ṣe àkọsílẹ̀ àwọn ènìyàn.

Ìtọpa dátà ò kí ń ṣe àwòran irú ènìyàn tí à ń ṣe. Àwọn ènìyàn máa ń ro ǹkan kan kí wọ́n sì sọ ìdàkejì rẹ̀, á ṣewọ́n bákan wọn ó sì hu ìwà míràn. Àwọn àsọtẹ́lẹ̀ ètò tàbí àwọn àṣa dígítà ò lè jíyìn fún àìlèsọ-àsọtẹ́lẹ̀ àti àmúdijú ìrírí ọmọ ènìyàn.
en: As an anthropologist, I believe that artificial intelligence and predictive analytics can be great to predict the course of a disease or to fight climate change. But we need to abandon the belief that these technologies can objectively profile humans and that we can rely on them to make data-driven decisions about individual lives. Because they can't profile humans.

Data traces are not the mirror of who we are. Humans think one thing and say the opposite, feel one way and act differently. Algorithmic predictions or our digital practices cannot account for the unpredictability and complexity of human experience.

passages.title: MENYO passage 829
paragraphs: Nígbà tí àwọn ẹ̀rọ bá ń kẹ́kọ̀ọ́, wọ́n máa ń kẹ́kọ̀ọ́ pẹ̀lu ètò aṣègbè, wọ́n sì máa ń kẹ́kọ̀ọ́ látara àkójọpọ̀ dátà aṣègbè. Lọ́wọ́lọ́wọ́ yìí, à ń rí àwọn àpẹẹrẹ ètò aṣègbè àkọ́kọ́. Díẹ̀ nínú àwọn àpẹrẹ wọ̀nyí ń dẹ́rù bani.

"Ní ọdún yìí, ilé-ìwe AI Now ní New York tí ṣe àtẹ̀jáde ìjábọ̀ kan tó fi hàn wí pé ìmọ̀-ẹ̀rọ AI tí wọ́n ń lò fún àsọtẹ́lẹ̀ ọlọ́pà ní wọ́n kọ́ pẹ̀lú dátà ""onídọ̀tí.""" Èyí jẹ́ dátà tí wọ́n ti gbà lásíkò ìtàn tí a mọ̀ fún ìṣegbè ẹlẹ́yámẹ̀yà àti àwọn ìṣesí ọlọ́pà tí ò fojú hàn. Nítorí dátà tó dọ̀tí ni wọ́n fi kọ́ àwọn ìmọ̀-ẹ̀rọ wọ̀nyí, wọn ò sọ tòótọ́, àbájáde wọn kò ń ṣàfikún àti àtúnṣe ìṣègbe ọlọ́pà àti àṣìṣe.
en: So when machines learn, they learn from biased algorithms, and they often learn from biased databases as well. At the moment, we're seeing the first examples of algorithmic bias. And some of these examples are frankly terrifying.

"This year, the AI Now Institute in New York published a report that revealed that the AI technologies that are being used for predictive policing have been trained on ""dirty"" data." This is basically data that had been gathered during historical periods of known racial bias and nontransparent police practices. Because these technologies are being trained with dirty data, they're not objective, and their outcomes are only amplifying and perpetrating police bias and error.

passages.title: MENYO passage 830
paragraphs: Ǹkan tí a nìlò báyìí ni ọ̀nà-àbáyọ òṣèlú. A fẹ́ kí ìjọba mọ̀ wí pé ẹ̀tọ ọmọ ènìyan wa ni ẹ̀to dátà wa. (àtẹ́wọ́ àti ariwo).

Àyàfi tí èyí bá ṣẹlẹ̀, a ò lè nírèti ọjọ́-iwájú adọ́gba. Mò ń ronú wí pé àwọn ọmọbìnrin mi máa kojú onírúúrú ètò ẹlẹ́yàmẹ̀yà àti àṣìṣe. Ṣé ẹ rí ìyàtọ̀ tó wà láàrín èmi àti àwọn ọmọbìrin mi ni wí pé kò sí àkọsílẹ̀ ìjọba níta níbẹ̀yẹn nípa ìgbà-èwe mi.
en: So what we need now is actually political solution. We need governments to recognize that our data rights are our human rights. (Applause and cheers)

Until this happens, we cannot hope for a more just future. I worry that my daughters are going to be exposed to all sorts of algorithmic discrimination and error. You see the difference between me and my daughters is that there's no public record out there of my childhood.

lessons.title: The Yorùbá alphabet
lessons.body:
Yorùbá is written with **25 letters**: a b d e ẹ f g gb h i j k l m n o ọ p r s ṣ t u w y.

There is **no c, q, v, x or z**. **gb** is one letter, made by saying g and b *at the same time*.

Three letters have a dot underneath, and each is a different letter from its plain version:
**ẹ** sounds like "e" in *bed*; **ọ** sounds like "aw" in *law*; **ṣ** sounds like "sh" in *shoe*.
Plain **e** is like "ay" in *day* (without the y glide), and plain **o** is like "o" in *go* (no w glide).

**p** is pronounced "kp" (k and p together), like gb but voiceless.

Typing tip: on the keyboard bar tap ẹ ọ ṣ, or type e. o. s. (letter + full stop).

exercises.prompt: Which letter is NOT in the Yorùbá alphabet?
exercises.explanation: Yorùbá has no c, q, v, x or z.

exercises.prompt: ẹ sounds like the vowel in…
ọ sounds like the vowel in…
How many letters does the Yorùbá alphabet have?
Type the letter that sounds like "sh"
exercises.hint: Use the ṣ key or type s.

lessons.title: The three tones
lessons.body:
Yorùbá is a **tone language**: every syllable is said on a pitch, and changing the pitch changes the word.

There are **three level tones**:
**High**: acute accent ´ (á é ẹ́ í ó ọ́ ú)
**Mid**: **no mark** (a e ẹ i o ọ u)
**Low**: grave accent ` (à è ẹ̀ ì ò ọ̀ ù)

A missing tone mark is not optional: unmarked means **mid**. In this app a wrong or missing tone mark is marked **wrong**, and it's counted separately so you can see your tone accuracy.

Example: **ọkọ** (mid-mid) = husband, **ọkọ́** (mid-high) = hoe, **ọkọ̀** (mid-low) = vehicle.

exercises.prompt: A vowel with no tone mark has which tone?

sources: Written for this app; tone marks checked against Wiktionary IPA (CC BY-SA)

lessons.title: Tone minimal sets
lessons.body:
The same letters can be up to four different words depending on tone:

**igbá** (mid-high): calabash
**igba** (mid-mid): two hundred
**ìgbà** (low-low): time, season
**ìgbá** (low-high): garden egg (bitter tomato)

**èdè** (low-low): language. **edé** (mid-high): shrimp/crayfish.

Read the marks every time. Reading Yorùbá without them means guessing between different words.
sources: Written for this app; tone marks checked against Wiktionary IPA (CC BY-SA)
Awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Nasal vowels, syllabic nasals and gliding tones
lessons.body:
**Nasal vowels** are written vowel + n: **an, ẹn, in, ọn, un**. The n is not pronounced as a separate n; the vowel is said through the nose. There is no nasal "on": the nasal o-sound is always written **ọn**.

**Syllabic nasals**: n or m can be a whole syllable with its own tone: **ń** (high), **ǹ** (low), and mid, which is written **n̄**. This is the one place where mid tone *is* marked. Example: **ó ń lọ** "he/she is going" (ń = high-tone progressive marker).

**Gliding tones**: a rising or falling pitch is written by doubling the vowel with two different marks, e.g. **káàárọ̀** (good morning): ká-à-á-rọ̀ = high-low-high-low.

exercises.prompt: In "ìyàn", how is the final "an" pronounced?
Which form marks a MID-tone syllabic nasal?
"ó ń lọ": what does ń show?

sources: Written for this app; tone marks checked against Wiktionary IPA (CC BY-SA)
Awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Tone in grammar
lessons.body:
Tone also carries grammar:

**ó** (high) = he/she/it as a subject: *Ó lọ* "He/She went."
After a **noun subject**, Yorùbá adds a **high-tone syllable** that copies the last vowel: *Adé lọ* is said *Adé é lọ*. You'll see it in speech-like writing; in standard writing it is often left out.

Negation **kò** (low) "not": *Ó kò lọ* is contracted to **Kò lọ** "He/She didn't go". With *o* "you": *o kò lọ* is contracted to **o ò lọ** "you didn't go".

In fast speech and in writing, vowels merge: **jẹ oúnjẹ** "eat food" becomes **jẹun**.

lessons.title: Respect: ẹ vs o, wọ́n vs ó
lessons.body:
Yorùbá grammar marks **respect**. Seniority goes by **age and status, not gender**. Someone even a few years older than you, an older sibling, a stranger or anyone in authority gets **honorific** forms.

**You**:
to a friend, a younger person or a child: **o** (subject), **ìwọ** (emphatic), **rẹ** ("your")
to an elder, a stranger, or several people: **ẹ** (subject), **ẹ̀yin** (emphatic), **yín** ("your" / "you" as object)

**He / she** (talking ABOUT someone):
a peer or younger person: **ó** (subject), **òun** (emphatic)
an elder or respected person: **wọ́n**, the plural "they", used for ONE person out of respect. Emphatic: **àwọn**.

Using **o** to an elder is not "casual"; it is **rude**. This app grades it as a **register error**.

Examples: *Kí ni orúkọ rẹ?* (to a child) vs *Kí ni orúkọ yín?* (to an elder) "What is your name?"
*Ó ti dé* "He/She has arrived" (a younger brother) vs *Wọ́n ti dé* "He/She has arrived" (your father).

exercises.prompt: You ask your friend's grandmother her name. Choose the right question.
exercises.explanation: yín shows respect to an elder; rẹ is for peers and younger people.

exercises.prompt: You ask a small child his name.
Your father has just come home. Tell someone "He has arrived".
exercises.explanation: Use honorific wọ́n when talking about a parent or elder.

exercises.prompt: Your younger brother has just come home. Tell someone "He has arrived".
Your older sister is 3 years older than you. Which "you" do you use with her?
exercises.explanation: Seniority is by age; even a slightly older sibling (ẹ̀gbọ́n) gets honorific forms.

exercises.prompt: Type the honorific word for "he/she" (talking about an elder)

lessons.title: Greetings by seniority
lessons.body:
Greeting is central in Yorùbá culture. To an elder you add **Ẹ** (respectful "you") in front of the greeting; to a peer or younger person you use the bare form.

**Ẹ káàárọ̀** / Káàárọ̀: good morning
**Ẹ káàsán** / Káàsán: good afternoon
**Ẹ kú alẹ́** / Kú alẹ́: good evening
**Ẹ kú iṣẹ́** / O kú iṣẹ́: well done (greeting someone at work)
**Ẹ kú àbọ̀** / Kú àbọ̀: welcome (back)
**Ẹ ṣé** / O ṣé: thank you (also *Ẹ ṣeun* / *O ṣeun*)
**Ẹ jọ̀ọ́** / Jọ̀ọ́: please

To be extra polite, add **mà** (to a woman, "ma'am") or **sà** (to a man, "sir"): *Ẹ káàárọ̀ mà.*

Don't greet an elder by their first name. Use a kinship or role word: **Bàbá** (father / older man), **Màmá** (mother / older woman), **Ẹ̀gbọ́n** (older sibling), **Ọ̀gá** (boss).

exercises.prompt: Morning. You meet your teacher (an older woman).
Morning. You meet your classmate (same age).
exercises.explanation: With peers the bare form is natural. Ẹ káàárọ̀ is not wrong but sounds distant.

exercises.prompt: An older man is working in his shop. Greet him.
Your aunt gives you food. Thank her.
Your younger cousin passes you the salt. Thank him.
Your grandfather returns from a trip. Welcome him.
How should you address your older brother, Túndé?
exercises.explanation: Calling an older person by their bare first name is disrespectful. Àbúrò means a YOUNGER sibling.

lessons.title: First sentences: I, you, aspect
lessons.body:
Yorùbá verbs don't change form. Time and aspect come from small words **before** the verb:

**ń** (high-tone nasal): ongoing. *Mo ń jẹun* "I am eating"
**ti**: completed. *Mo ti jẹun* "I have eaten"
**máa** / **yóò**: future. *Mo máa lọ* / *Màá lọ* "I will go"

Subject pronouns: **mo** I · **o** you (familiar) · **ó** he/she/it · **a** we · **ẹ** you (plural/respectful) · **wọ́n** they / he-she (honorific)

Word order is Subject-Verb-Object, like English: *Mo fẹ́ omi* "I want water".

options: I am going to the market
I will go to the market
exercises.answer: I am going to the market

sources: Written for this app; tone marks checked against Wiktionary IPA (CC BY-SA)

lessons.title: Asking questions
lessons.body:
Question words usually come first and are often followed by **ni**:
**Kí ni…?** What…? *Kí ni orúkọ rẹ?* "What is your name?"
**Ta ni…?** Who…? *Ta ni olùkọ́ yín?* "Who is your teacher?"
**Níbo ni…?** Where…? *Níbo ni o ń lọ?* "Where are you going?"
**Báwo ni…?** How…? *Báwo ni?* "How are things?"
**Èló ni?** How much (is it)? (at the market)
**Nígbà wo ni…?** When…?
**Ṣé…?** turns a statement into a yes/no question: *Ṣé o ti jẹun?* "Have you eaten?"

exercises.prompt: Which word makes a yes/no question?

sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Possession: my, your, his…
lessons.body:
The owner comes **after** the thing owned:
**ilé mi** my house · **ilé rẹ** your house (familiar) · **ilé rẹ̀** his/her house · **ilé wa** our house · **ilé yín** your house (plural or respectful) · **ilé wọn** their house / his-her house (respectful)
Note the tone: **rẹ** (mid) = your; **rẹ̀** (low) = his/her. A tone mark changes the person!
Noun + noun works the same way: *ilé Túndé* "Tunde's house", *ọmọ ọba* "the king's child".
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: "To be": jẹ́, ni, wà, and describing words
lessons.body:
Yorùbá splits English "to be" into several words:
**jẹ́**: identity: *Mo jẹ́ olùkọ́* "I am a teacher."
**ni** (focus, very common): *Olùkọ́ ni mí* "I am a teacher" (lit. "a teacher is me").
**wà**: exist / be located: *Ó wà nílé* "He/she is at home."
Many describing words are **verbs**, so no "be" is needed: *Ó dára* "It is good." *Ó tóbi* "It is big." *Ó ga* "He/she is tall."
"There isn't / he isn't here": **Kò sí**.

exercises.explanation: dára is itself a verb: "be good".

sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Saying "not"
lessons.body:
**kò** not (past/present): *Kò lọ* "He/she didn't go." With *mo* "I": *Mi ò lọ* / *Èmi kò lọ* "I didn't go."
**kò ní** will not: *Mi ò ní lọ* "I won't go."
**kì í** does not (habitually): *Kì í mu ọtí* "He/she doesn't drink alcohol."
**kì í ṣe** is not (identity): *Kì í ṣe olùkọ́* "He/she is not a teacher."
**má** don't (command): *Má lọ!* "Don't go!" To an elder: *Ẹ má lọ.*
Common phrase: *Mi ò mọ̀* "I don't know."
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Numbers 1–10
lessons.body:
Yorùbá numbers have a **counting form** and a **describing form** (after a noun):
1 ọ̀kan / kan · 2 èjì / méjì · 3 ẹ̀ta / mẹ́ta · 4 ẹ̀rin / mẹ́rin · 5 àrún / márùn-ún · 6 ẹ̀fà / mẹ́fà · 7 èje / méje · 8 ẹ̀jọ / mẹ́jọ · 9 ẹ̀sán / mẹ́sàn-án · 10 ẹ̀wá / mẹ́wàá
*ọmọ kan* "one child", *ọmọ méjì* "two children", *ìwé mẹ́ta* "three books".
Tone marks matter here too. Watch them carefully.
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Time and aspect: ti, ń, máa ń, máa, kò tíì
lessons.body:
Yorùbá marks *how* an action happens with small words before the verb:
**ti** completed: *Mo ti jẹun* "I have eaten."
**ń** ongoing: *Mo ń jẹun* "I am eating."
**máa ń** habitual: *Mo máa ń jẹ ìrẹsì* "I (usually) eat rice."
**máa / yóò / á** future: *Mo máa lọ* · *Èmi yóò lọ* · *Màá lọ* "I will go."
**kò tíì** not yet: *Kò tíì dé* "He/she hasn't arrived yet."
A bare verb usually means a completed past event: *Mo lọ* "I went."
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Commands and polite requests
lessons.body:
A bare verb is a command: *Wá!* "Come!" *Jókòó!* "Sit!" Fine with children and close friends.
To elders and strangers, always use **ẹ** + verb, often with **Ẹ jọ̀ọ́** "please": *Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ jókòó* "Please sit down."
Negative: **Má** (familiar) / **Ẹ má** (respectful): *Ẹ má bínú* "Sorry / please don't be upset."
"Give me…": *Fún mi ní omi* "Give me water" → politely *Ẹ jọ̀ọ́, ẹ fún mi ní omi.*

exercises.prompt: Ask an elderly visitor to sit down.
You bumped into an older woman. Apologise.

sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Place words: ní, sí, láti, nínú, lórí…
lessons.body:
**ní** at/in (no movement) · **sí** to (movement) · **láti** from · **fún** for · **pẹ̀lú** with
**nínú** inside · **lórí** on top of · **lábẹ́** under · **lẹ́yìn** behind / after · **níwájú** in front of
*Mo ń lọ sí ọjà* "I'm going to the market." *Ìwé wà lórí tábìlì* "The book is on the table."
**ní** often merges with the next word: ní ilé → **nílé**, ní ọjà → **lọ́jà** (n → l before a vowel other than i).
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Verb chains (serial verbs)
lessons.body:
Yorùbá often strings verbs together where English uses one verb or a preposition:
*Ó mú ìwé wá* "He/she brought the book" (lit. took book came).
*Mo ra ẹja jẹ* "I bought fish and ate it."
*Gbé e wá* "Bring it here" (lit. carry it come).
*Ó sáré lọ* "He/she ran away" (lit. ran went).
When translating into English, merge the chain into natural English.
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Comparisons: ju … lọ
lessons.body:
**X + describing verb + ju + Y + lọ**: *Adé ga ju Túndé lọ* "Ade is taller than Tunde."
**jù lọ** = the most: *Òun ló ga jù lọ* "He/she is the tallest."
**bí** / **bíi** = like / as: *Ó ga bí bàbá rẹ̀* "He's as tall as his father."
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Building words with prefixes
lessons.body:
Many nouns are built from verbs and phrases:
**oní-** "owner / person with": *onílé* landlord (ilé = house), *oníṣòwò* trader
**olù-** "one who does": *olùkọ́* teacher (kọ́ = teach)
**a-** "one who": *akẹ́kọ̀ọ́* student (kọ́ ẹ̀kọ́ = learn a lesson)
**ì- / à-** turn verbs into nouns: *ìfẹ́* love (fẹ́ = love)
**àì-** "not / lack of": *àìsàn* illness (sàn = get well), *àìmọ̀* ignorance (mọ̀ = know)
Recognising these lets you guess new words while reading.
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Days and times of day
lessons.body:
Times of day: **àárọ̀** morning · **ọ̀sán** afternoon · **ìrọ̀lẹ́** evening · **alẹ́** night (hence *Ẹ káàárọ̀, Ẹ káàsán, Ẹ kú alẹ́*).
Days (traditional names): Ọjọ́ Àìkú (Sunday) · Ọjọ́ Ajé (Monday) · Ọjọ́ Ìṣẹ́gun (Tuesday) · Ọjọ́rú (Wednesday) · Ọjọ́bọ̀ (Thursday) · Ọjọ́ Ẹtì (Friday) · Ọjọ́ Àbámẹ́ta (Saturday).
**lónìí** today · **lánàá** yesterday · **lọ́la** tomorrow (from ní + òní / àná / ọ̀la).
*Day names vary somewhat by region; native-speaker check pending.*
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Relative clauses with tí
lessons.body:
**tí** = who / which / that, placed after the noun:
*ọkùnrin tí ó wá* → usually **ọkùnrin tó wá** "the man who came" (tí + ó → **tó**)
*ìwé tí mo rà* "the book (that) I bought"
*ibi tí a ń lọ* "the place where we're going"
With **náà** "the (aforementioned)": *ọkùnrin tó wá náà* "the man who came."

exercises.prompt: "tó" in "ọkùnrin tó wá" is a contraction of…

options: the place where we are going
exercises.answer: the place where we are going

sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Focus with ni ("It was X who…")
lessons.body:
To highlight something, move it to the front and add **ni**:
*Adé wá* "Ade came" → **Adé ni ó wá** → **Adé ló wá** "It was ADE who came." (ni + ó → **ló**)
*Ìwé ni mo rà* "It was a BOOK that I bought."
*Lánàá ni wọ́n dé* "It was YESTERDAY that they arrived."
Question words use the same pattern: *Kí ni o rà?* "What did you buy?"
Translate focus into natural English emphasis, not always "it was…".

options: It was a book that I bought
Is it a book I bought?
exercises.answer: It was a book that I bought

sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: "If" and "when": bí/tí … bá
lessons.body:
**Bí / Tí + subject + bá + verb** = "if": *Tí òjò bá rọ̀, mi ò ní lọ* "If it rains, I won't go."
*Bí o bá wá, a máa lọ papọ̀* "If you come, we'll go together."
**nígbà tí** = when: *Nígbà tí mo dé, wọ́n ti lọ* "When I arrived, they had left."
**kí … tó** = before: *Kí o tó lọ, jẹun* "Before you go, eat."
**lẹ́yìn tí** = after.
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Reported speech and òun
lessons.body:
**pé** = "that": *Ó sọ pé òun ti dé* "He/she said that he/she has arrived."
Yorùbá has a special pronoun for reported speech: **òun** refers back to **the speaker being reported**, while **ó** refers to **someone else**:
*Adé sọ pé òun máa wá* "Ade said that he (Ade himself) will come."
*Adé sọ pé ó máa wá* "Ade said that he/she (someone else) will come."
This distinction is invisible in English, so read carefully when translating.
**kí** = "that (should)" for wishes and requests: *Mo fẹ́ kí o wá* "I want you to come."

exercises.prompt: "Adé sọ pé òun máa wá": who will come?

sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Split verbs (ba … jẹ́)
lessons.body:
Some verbs split around their object:
**ba … jẹ́** spoil: *Ó ba iṣẹ́ náà jẹ́* "He/she spoiled the work." Without an object they join: *Ọkọ̀ náà ti bàjẹ́* "The vehicle has broken down."
**rán … létí** remind: *Rán mi létí* "Remind me."
**fi … sílẹ̀** leave/put down: *Fi í sílẹ̀* "Leave it."
When you meet a verb that seems to have no ending, look for its other half later in the sentence.

exercises.prompt: In "Ó ba iṣẹ́ náà jẹ́", the verb is…

sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Because, so, but, and
lessons.body:
**nítorí pé / torí pé** because · **nítorí náà** therefore · **ṣùgbọ́n** but · **tàbí** or · **bákan náà** likewise/also
**"and"**: **àti** joins nouns (*bàbá àti màmá*); **sì** joins clauses (*Ó jẹun, ó sì sùn* "He ate and slept").
*Mi ò lọ nítorí pé òjò ń rọ̀* "I didn't go because it was raining."
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Reading merged words (elision)
lessons.body:
In natural writing, vowels meet and one drops. Expand them in your head when reading:
ní ilé → **nílé** · ní ọjà → **lọ́jà** · ní òní → **lónìí** · jẹ oúnjẹ → **jẹun** · ra ẹja → **rẹja** · wá sí ilé → **wá sílé** · tí ó → **tó** · ni ó → **ló**
The surviving vowel keeps its tone, and the merged word often keeps the tone of the dropped syllable too, so tone marks on merged words still matter.
Exam texts and MENYO passages use these contractions often.
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: English passives in Yorùbá: impersonal wọ́n
lessons.body:
Yorùbá has no true passive. It uses **wọ́n** "they" with no specific person:
*Wọ́n jí ọkọ̀ mi* "My car was stolen" (lit. they stole my car).
*Wọ́n bí i ní Èkó* "He/she was born in Lagos."
*Wọ́n sọ pé…* "It is said that…"
Remember: **wọ́n** can also be the respectful "he/she", so use context to decide between "they", an elder, or a passive.

exercises.prompt: "Wọ́n jí ọkọ̀ mi" is best translated…

sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Formal writing and titles
lessons.body:
Formal letters and official texts use **respect forms throughout**: ẹ / yín for "you", wọ́n / wọn for an honoured third person.
Titles: **Ọ̀gbẹ́ni** Mr. · **Ìyáàfin** Mrs. · **Arábìnrin** Miss/Ms. · **Ọ̀mọ̀wé** Dr. (scholar) · **Olóyè** Chief.
Express thanks and good wishes respectfully: *Ẹ ṣé púpọ̀* "Thank you very much."
In a translation exam, a formal passage translated with familiar forms (o, rẹ, ó for an elder) is marked as a register error.

exercises.prompt: Thanking a school principal in a formal letter

sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Repetition for meaning
lessons.body:
Repeating a word changes its meaning:
*díẹ̀* a little → **díẹ̀díẹ̀** little by little, slowly · *dáadáa* well · **kíákíá** quickly
Numbers: *méjì* two → **méjì méjì** two by two / two each
Verb → noun: *lọ* go → *lílọ* going; *wá* come → *wíwá* coming (the first consonant + i with high tone is added).
*Ẹ máa rìn díẹ̀díẹ̀* "Walk slowly."
sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Proverbs (òwe)
lessons.body:
Proverbs are central to educated Yorùbá speech and writing. A famous saying about proverbs themselves:
**Òwe lẹṣin ọ̀rọ̀; bí ọ̀rọ̀ bá sọnù, òwe la fi ń wá a.** "A proverb is the horse of speech; when words are lost, we use proverbs to find them."
**Ìka kò dọ́gba.** "Fingers are not equal": people differ in ability and fortune.
**Àgbà kì í wà lọ́jà kí orí ọmọ tuntun wọ́.** "An elder does not stay in the market and let a newborn's head be crooked": elders are responsible for guiding the young.
Translate the *meaning*, and keep the image when it's clear in English.
*Wording of proverbs varies; check with a native speaker.*

options: People are not all the same
exercises.answer: People are not all the same

exercises.prompt: The proverb about the elder in the market teaches…

sources: Written for this app; awaiting native-speaker review

lessons.title: Reading text without tone marks
lessons.body:
Much real-world Yorùbá (social media, signs, some newspapers) leaves out tone marks and even underdots. Then *oko* could be **ọkọ** (husband), **ọkọ̀** (vehicle), **ọkọ́** (hoe) or **oko** (farm).
Strategy: (1) use the surrounding words: *wa oko* "drive a vehicle" vs *lọ sí oko* "go to the farm"; (2) check the dictionary for all toned versions; (3) when writing, always restore full marks.
This app only uses properly marked text in lessons and exams. Passages that fail the check are flagged ⚠.

exercises.prompt: Unmarked "oko" in "Mo lọ sí oko láti ṣiṣẹ́" (I went to the ___ to work) is most likely…
Unmarked "oko" in "Ó wa oko lọ sí Èkó" (He drove the ___ to Lagos) is most likely…

lessons.title: Large numbers (base 20)
lessons.body:
Traditional Yorùbá counts in **twenties**, and some numbers are formed by subtraction:
20 **ogún** · 30 **ọgbọ̀n** · 40 **ogójì** (2 × 20) · 60 **ọgọ́ta** (3 × 20) · 80 **ọgọ́rin** · 100 **ọgọ́rùn-ún** · 200 **igba** · 1000 **ẹgbẹ̀rún**
15 is "five less than twenty" and 25 is "five less than thirty": the subtractive pattern runs through the system.
In modern life, large numbers (prices, dates) are often said in English, but older texts and formal writing use the traditional forms.
*Number words: native-speaker check pending.*

lessons.title: Translating paragraphs
lessons.body:
Yorùbá → English:
• **ó** has no gender: choose he/she/it from context. Honorific **wọ́n** for one person → "he/she", not "they".
• Aspect, not tense: a bare verb is usually past; **ń** can be present or past progressive.
• Serial verbs → one English verb (*mú … wá* = bring).
• Focus **ni** → English emphasis or "it was … who".
• Expand contractions (nílé, ló, tó) before translating.
English → Yorùbá: decide the **register** first (who is addressed?), then mark every tone and underdot. The certification exam checks both.

exercises.prompt: "Bàbá wọ́n ti dé" (about one respected man): "wọ́n" →

options: He took water and came separately
